claims.text: The target non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs have densities below 6 g/cm³.
The initial microstructure contains metastable solid-solution regions together with stable intermetallic compounds.
A homogeneous Mg distribution and a compositional Mg gradient can be produced as the controlled comparison.
The compositional gradient creates regions of elevated initial Mg supersaturation.
The homogeneous and gradient samples will be exposed to approximately 700°C in an oxidizing atmosphere.
The homogeneous and gradient samples will also be exposed to salt spray or NaCl solution.
Regions with greater initial Mg supersaturation undergo selective, diffusion-driven oxidation during high-temperature and corrosive exposures.
Mg diffuses out of metastable solid-solution regions during exposure.
Mg preferentially oxidizes at phase boundaries.
Diffusion-driven oxidation promotes nucleation and growth of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Exposure produces a continuous or semi-continuous Mg-rich oxide layer at microstructural interfaces.
The Mg-rich oxide/intermetallic interface alters alloy passivation behavior and structural stability.
Gradient samples will evolve more strongly toward Mg-rich oxide and intermetallic phases than homogeneous samples.
An effective Mg-rich oxide layer may improve corrosion resistance through passivation.
Disruption of the Mg-rich oxide layer may instead accelerate degradation.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys whose initial processing yields a mixture of metastable and stable phases.
No significant difference in Mg-rich interface formation or in corrosion and oxidation behavior between the two sample sets would falsify the hypothesis.
